title: I am sorry to say this , but , Killers of The Flower Moon is dreadfully boring

commenti.body: [removed]

I think you wanted a different kind of movie than Scorsese was making. Nothing wrong with not liking it- but this is not suppose to be “entertaining” or “thrilling” like the other examples you gave. It’s a deliberately miserable and educational tale that exposes its viewers to a lot of dark themes to reflect on, and perhaps reconsider some viewpoints about some highly contentious topics in society today. 

If I’m correct in my estimation of Scorsese’s intent, I think he was successful in delivering. I found a lot to think about in that movie and the elements that make it a difficult watch are, in my opinion, crucial to making it effective.

>It might have worked better, if the original plan of having Leo play the FBI investigator , was used. The mystery wasn't there.

The whole point of the film is that it's not a mystery. Hale is open about being a racist monster (in front of his family) and the audience is aware of his plot 20-30 minutes into the film. Scorsese and Leo have talked about how the initial drafts of the script did focus more on the FBI and a mystery-driven plot but that it felt wrong, left out too much of the Osage's story and turned it into a white savior narrative about the FBI heroically coming in and cracking the case.

The film is paced fairly slowly, but again that's on purpose. Not to appeal to authority but Thelma Schoonmaker certainly knows more about pacing a film than you do. The film isn't supposed to be exciting the way some of Scorsese's older films are, it's very confrontational in how it addresses the audience and forces you to see the depravity of Hale and his conspirators. Scorsese didn't want to people to leave thinking Hale or Burkhart were anything but despicable, cowardly monsters like the way people sometimes idolize Jordan Belfort or some of his other protagonists.

I thought DiCaprio's character lacked agency and generally went along with either Hale or Mollie depending on who was physically present. Got tired of him making the same pained expression every time he was pressured into doing something or admitting something.

Hale seemed like a generic gangster who never admits anything and is completely without remorse. Mollie was interesting but mostly disappeared for the last portion of the movie.

It felt like the movie was trying to avoid embellishment in order to be historically accurate, which meant the characters were underdeveloped and the story suffered.

Most of all, it felt like it was trying to tell the kind of story that The Wire told about Baltimore, only there was never going to be enough time for that. It was the same basic plot of the police/FBI moving up the ladder to get to the crime boss, only without the kind of character development and exploration of the root causes behind the crimes.

Most true crime media tends to turn tragedy into a sort of sport - when people are focused on unraveling a mystery, it’s easy to lose sight of the tragedy that occurred. That, in itself, would be a tragedy for a true story as harrowing as this, so I think Scorsese made the right move in allowing the movie to dwell on that tragedy and anger towards the murderers and their enablers.

However, that approach does not make for an exciting watch. That said, I personally didn't find it dull or boring - the movie didn't surprise me or keep me on the edge of my seat, but I was consistently engaged.

Despite that, though, the movie still felt overlong to me and I was very much feeling the movie's runtime in the third act. I think it'd be hard to get this movie under 3 hours, but every little bit helps.

Slower films set a pace where you can get out of your own head and get into the characters you're watching more deeply then you can if it's all snappy dialogue and fast edits. you also can reflect on what you're seeing as you're seeing it. 

The contrast between the Osage not being the type of people who want to take advantage of someone else and the blatant manipulation that Hale and everyone he got to do his bidding exhibit is so stark. you can see why he was able to do what he did. seeing that happen over and over over a long period of time makes it all the more painful and upsetting.

The most chilling moment for me was when Hale says in prison that everyone will move on and no one will care or remember this. Sitting in a theater in 2023 and most of the audience learning the story for the first time proves his point. it makes you think about human nature and how we seem to purposely refuse to learn from the past and how the majority of good people seem unable to stop the few truly malevolent among us to cause incredible harm. Hale was just like an Escobar, doing good things for the community to cover up his true priorities; both also do all of this evil for the pathetic goal of amassing money.

to me, Leo was too old for this role - he didn't seem like a young man who came fresh-faced out of world war I, he seemed like a middle-aged guy, which made his confusion over what was happening around him seem really simple-minded instead of naive. It didn't ruin the movie for me as it's a frequent thing that happens with casting but I think it would have been better with a younger man in that role.

Hale actually was outwardly not remorseful his whole life. That has been noted

This pacing fits the source material and events being told. You could mention the same from other crime dramas of his. I know people that expected The Irishman to be more dynamic and stopped halfway as they couldn’t bear the pacing. Definitely not the film to pick if you are looking for something more along the lines of Goodfellas / Departed. It worked imo, but certainly a slow burning one

I thought it was fantastic, rewatching a lot of Scorsese's work this year but I think it'll be right up there for me - if not top 5, then close.

It seems like a spiritual companion piece to Silence and The Irishman to me. More contemplative, less fast-paced, in many ways more concerned with consequences than actions

I thought Leo was good, and De Niro and Gladstone fantastic. Pacing was fine, it wasn't the kind of film that flies by in what feels like half the time, but I never got the impression it was meant to be. It feels its length but didn't drag and didn't lose interest for me 

Disclaimer that I read the book and knew most of the details going in, and was thoroughly engaged with the smaller scale, more personal story. The Osage & their history are much more interesting to me than another FBI tale.

>Scorsese and Leo have talked about how the initial drafts of the script did focus more on the FBI and a mystery-driven plot but that it felt wrong, left out too much of the Osage's story and turned it into a white savior narrative about the FBI heroically coming in and cracking the case.



That's basically how the book is. I haven't seen the movie yet but I'm glad they changed the structure from that.

"Not to appeal to authority but" *appeals to authority*

While OP clearly cant name a single slow film he enjoys for the life of him, I dont think it's unfair for him not to enjoy a deliberately grim depressing 3.5h education about horrors commited against native americans. 

I respect KOTFM and found enough cinematic merit in there to enjoy it as well, but I do feel it's the first time in Scorsese's career he prioritized making an 'important' film over a good one.
The part of the source material about the atrocities is only like 100 pages long so not really

Not all art is meant to be enjoyable, I'm not sure what else to say. Whether or not you think the film is "good" is subjective but I've seen so many people criticize it for being slow or uncomfortable to watch which is *exactly* the point. It's like watching Salo and complaining that the film makes fascism look *too* depraved and dehumanizing
I think the seriousness of KOFT fits nicely within the more trend of his more recent works like The Irishman and Silence.
absolutely agree, it was a typical Scorcese film

I half agree. The slow pace before the FBl shows up creates a perfect feeling of inescapable dread.

But once Jesse Plemons arrives, all that needs to happen is: (a) uncovering the conspiracy, (b) saving Mollie, (c) Mollie confronting Ernest and he lies, (d) the Lucky Strike epilogue. 

The extended procedural uncovering the case, then the long courtroom sequences go on forever and don’t add to the thematic argument of the movie. Cut that down and the movie plays far better.

I think that's a fair criticism of Salo too, that movie is essentially performance art anyway

>Scorsese didn't want to people to leave thinking Hale or Burkhart were anything but despicable, cowardly monsters like the way people sometimes idolize Jordan Belfort or some of his other protagonists.

Therein lies why a lot of fans of Scorsese aren't feeling this one. Historically he doesn't have an agenda for guiding how the audience should feel about a character and their actions. His usual style is to step back and let the audience decide what's right and wrong in the given situation. Some people end up sympathizing with the destructive and dysfunction characters, and so what? That's art. Holding the audience's hand makes things less interesting and authentic feeling.
